prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B016 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case rests on a discovery chain that is original and independently confirmed: proglucagon processing, the identification of the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and the human physiology of its secretion and action. It is mature, and its consequences are now documented in large randomized trials of glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened this. All six files prefer B016, and the real disagreement is the third name, which is a question of principle and not of support counts. The principle I would apply is that this prize honours the discovery of what the hormone is and does and which form is active, and that the drug class is its demonstrated consequence. On that principle Drucker (physiology of the peptide and its actions), Holst (secretion, the incretin effect and human physiology) and Mojsov (identification of the active peptide form) each hold a distinct step in the chain. I keep the prize as one part. A second part would add an attribution burden (Walter and Mori are clean, but optogenetics, TOR and CAR-T are not) without improving the case for the first, and nothing in round 1 shows that a second part is needed to do justice to B016.
statement.case_against: Credit remains the weak point. Four credited names compete for three seats and Habener, outside the supplied list, may have a priority claim on the active peptide that I cannot settle from the files I may read. A citation limited to physiology can be read as overlooking Knudsen's acylated analogue, which made the therapy practical, and sandberg-rickard's reading of the prize as covering physiology to therapy is a legitimate one. Long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy are still accumulating, and a GLP-1 prize risks looking like an endorsement of a commercial drug program. Finally, a single-part prize on a candidate everyone ranks highly is a convenient outcome, and I have tried to test it against B010 rather than assume it.

responses.point: Sandberg now prefers B016 with Holst, Drucker and Knudsen, and a citation that covers both GLP-1 physiology and the development of long-acting therapies, while still regarding the unfolded protein response as the cleanest discovery on the list.
responses.response: I take the Knudsen argument seriously, and your round-1 file states the tension honestly: choosing Knudsen undervalues identification of the active peptide, and choosing Mojsov undervalues the step that turned the biology into a medicine. We agree that one of the four must go. I come down on the discovery side because the citation you propose would turn a prize for physiology into a prize for a drug program, and because the identification of the active form is what made later analogue design possible at all. I do not think this is a judgment against development work as such. If the committee majority decides that the medicine is the achievement, then Knudsen replaces Mojsov and I would not regard that as an error of science. On B010, I agree with you that it is the cleanest discovery and the strongest alternative. Its distance from patients is what keeps me from putting it first, not any doubt about the work.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved from Knudsen in her opening to Mojsov in round 1, says the prize is for discovery, and asks that the scientific case be tested instead of accepted by consensus.
responses.response: I share your move and your reasoning, and I take your point about consensus by default. To test it, I asked what would change my preference. If the dated record showed that Mojsov's identification of the active peptide was not independent or not first, I would swap in Knudsen or reconsider the third seat, because the argument for her rests entirely on that step being a real discovery contribution. I cannot verify that from the files I may use, and neither can you. So I state my position as conditional: Mojsov on the present best reading, with the attribution uncertainty acknowledged openly, not hidden behind six matching preferred configurations. I would also ask that the citation say 'identification of its active form' and not claim exclusive priority for the peptide, which keeps the wording defensible if the record is contested.

responses.point: Perlmann supports Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, says a public dispute is not evidence of priority order, and notes that his hesitation about B010 concerns its distance from disease and not its quality.
responses.response: I agree that controversy is not evidence and that the credit should be settled against the dated primary literature, not against how loudly it has been argued. That is why I keep Mojsov in the trio only on the basis of the scientific step she is credited with and not on public sentiment. On B010, your point about distance from disease is also mine, but I would not make it decisive for a Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine, since the prize has often honoured basic mechanism. That is why I hold B010 as my first alternative. It remains a strong, mature pair of discoveries, and it is the first place I would look if the GLP-1 allocation cannot be settled.

responses.point: El Manira prefers the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio and ranks optogenetics second, and notes that any three of the six credited names would exclude people with decisive contributions.
responses.response: I agree that B044 has the most serious attribution problem on the shortlist. The microbial channelrhodopsin discovery, its demonstration of function in neurons and the deployment in behaving animals are separate steps with different people, and a three-person cut either breaks the chain or excludes someone whose work was decisive. That is the main reason I keep it as my second alternative and not in a two-part configuration. I would reconsider only if the committee could define the part narrowly (for example, the discovery and characterization of channelrhodopsin as a light-gated channel) so that the credited names follow the step cleanly. I have not seen that case made in round 1, and adding the part now would weaken a prize that is otherwise well defined.

responses.point: Linnarsson's round-1 configuration names Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and he states that the science does not depend on support counts, but that the clinical story may overshadow the physiological discovery the citation should honour.
responses.response: Your configuration settles the chair's question in my reading: your file names Mojsov, so the count is five to one for the trio, although the comments in other files assumed otherwise. I accept your concern that the clinical story can overshadow the physiology, and I have tried to answer it in my citation, which leads with the physiology and the active form and presents the therapies as what the discovery enabled. I also agree with you that the three-person limit should not be stretched. Where I differ slightly is on the fallback. You name B010 and B023 as alternatives, and I keep B010 and B044, because I rank CAR-T below both on the credit problem raised by earlier chimeric-receptor work.

uncertainties: The priority record for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, including Habener and others outside the supplied credit, is not verified from the files I may read. My position on the third name is conditional on Mojsov's identification of the active form holding up against the dated literature.
Whether the committee majority sees the prize as honouring discovery or the full arc to therapy, which decides between Mojsov and Knudsen.
Long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy are still accumulating.
Whether a second part (B010 first) would add real scientific value or only add attribution risk; I judge the latter but the case for B010 as a stand-alone achievement is strong.
statement.conflict_note: No change. My profile records about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann and a postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard. Neither is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot, so I do not see a recusal issue. I have no documented involvement with Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, Walter, Mori or any other credited person.
